title: Electron Spin and Magnetic Moment
short_intro: Electron spin is an intrinsic form of angular momentum possessed by electrons, independent of their orbital motion. It is characterized by a spin quantum number s = 1/2 and accounts for fine structure and magnetic properties in atomic systems.

exam_scope.tgt_core: Definition of spin quantum numbers, Pauli's Exclusion Principle, fundamental postulates, and qualitative understanding of the Stern-Gerlach experiment.
exam_scope.pgt_extension: Quantitative treatment of spin-orbit coupling, gyromagnetic ratio for spin, spin magnetic moment, vector model of the atom, and total angular momentum.

prerequisites: Spatial quantization and space quantization rules
Orbital angular momentum and magnetic quantum numbers

concept_notes.heading: Discovery and Postulation of Electron Spin
bullets: Proposed by Samuel Goudsmit and George Uhlenbeck in 1925 to explain anomalies in alkali metal atomic spectra (doublets).
Assigned an intrinsic angular momentum vector S that cannot be reduced to classical rotation of a finite charge distribution.
The magnitude of spin angular momentum is given by S = √(s(s+1)) ℏ where s = 1/2.

concept_notes.heading: Spin Quantum Numbers and Spatial Quantization
bullets: The spin quantum number s is fixed at 1/2 for an electron.
The z-component of spin angular momentum is quantized as S<sub>z</sub> = m<sub>s</sub> ℏ, where m<sub>s</sub> = ±1/2.
This leads to two possible spin orientations in a magnetic field: 'spin-up' (m<sub>s</sub> = +1/2) and 'spin-down' (m<sub>s</sub> = -1/2).

concept_notes.heading: Spin Magnetic Moment and Gyromagnetic Ratio
bullets: Associated with spin angular momentum is an intrinsic magnetic dipole moment μs.
The ratio of spin magnetic moment to spin angular momentum is twice that of orbital motion, expressed by the Landé g-factor for spin g<sub>s</sub> ≈ 2.
Expressed mathematically as μs = - gs (μB / ℏ) S, where μB is the Bohr magneton.

concept_notes.heading: Pauli's Exclusion Principle and Spin Statistics
bullets: States that no two identical fermions (such as electrons) can occupy the same quantum state simultaneously.
Requires the total wavefunction of a multi-electron system to be antisymmetric under the exchange of any two electrons.
Directly accounts for the periodic table structure and electron shell capacities (2n<sup>2</sup>).

derivations.title: Magnitude and Component of Spin Angular Momentum
derivations.conditions: Quantum mechanical treatment of spin-1/2 particles
steps: Write the general operator equation for angular momentum squared: S<sup>2</sup>|s, m<sub>s</sub>> = s(s+1)ℏ<sup>2</sup>|s, m<sub>s</sub>>.
Substitute the value of spin quantum number s = 1/2 into the eigenvalue equation.
Apply the z-component operator: S<sub>z</sub>|s, m<sub>s</sub>> = m<sub>s</sub>ℏ|s, m<sub>s</sub>> with m<sub>s</sub> = ±1/2.

derivations.title: Spin Magnetic Dipole Moment of an Electron
derivations.conditions: Relativistic quantum mechanics (Dirac equation implication) or semi-classical relation with g<sub>s</sub> = 2
steps: Start with the definition of magnetic dipole moment in terms of angular momentum: \vec{\mu}_s = -\frac{e}{2m} g_s \vec{S}.
Substitute the electron mass m = m<sub>e</sub>, charge magnitude e, and spin g-factor g<sub>s</sub> = 2.
Express in terms of Bohr magneton μ<sub>B</sub> = eℏ/2m<sub>e</sub> by utilizing S = (ℏ/2): \vec{\mu}_s = -2 \left(\frac{\mu_B}{\hbar}\right) \vec{S}.

graphs_and_experiments.title: Stern-Gerlach Experiment Setup
graphs_and_experiments.what_to_draw: A beam of neutral silver atoms passing through an inhomogeneous magnetic field created by pole pieces of specific shape (one flat, one sharp edge), resulting in the splitting of the beam into two distinct traces on a collector plate.
graphs_and_experiments.interpretation: Proves the space quantization of electron spin. Instead of a continuous smear, the atomic beam splits into exactly two paths corresponding to m<sub>s</sub> = +1/2 and m<sub>s</sub> = -1/2.
graphs_and_experiments.exam_use: Frequently asked in conceptual and descriptive questions regarding the physical proof of electron spin and space quantization.

graphs_and_experiments.title: Vector Model of Spin Quantization
graphs_and_experiments.what_to_draw: A cone of possible orientations of the spin vector S around the z-axis, showing vector magnitude √(3/4)ℏ and discrete projections along the z-axis at +(1/2)ℏ and -(1/2)ℏ.
graphs_and_experiments.interpretation: Demonstrates that while the magnitude and z-component are precisely known, the x and y components remain uncertain due to Heisenberg's uncertainty principle.
graphs_and_experiments.exam_use: Tested in PGT multiple-choice questions regarding allowed projections and angle calculations.

graphs_and_experiments.title: Potential Energy vs Position in Stern-Gerlach Inhomogeneous Field
graphs_and_experiments.what_to_draw: A linear splitting graph where atoms with spin-up experience upward force and spin-down experience downward force proportional to the field gradient.
graphs_and_experiments.interpretation: Illustrates the spatial separation of magnetic dipoles based on their orientation relative to the external field gradient.
graphs_and_experiments.exam_use: Used in numerical problems calculating deflection distance and force.

solved_numericals.question: Calculate the magnitude of the spin angular momentum of an electron.
solution_steps: Identify the spin quantum number for an electron: s = 1/2.
Write the formula for spin angular momentum magnitude: S = \sqrt{s(s+1)}\hbar.
Substitute s = 1/2 into the formula: S = \sqrt{\frac{1}{2}\left(\frac{1}{2} + 1\right)}\hbar = \sqrt{\frac{3}{4}}\hbar.
Compute the numerical value: S = \frac{\sqrt{3}}{2} \times 1.054 \times 10^{-34} \text{ J s}.

solved_numericals.question: Find the maximum z-component of the spin magnetic moment of an electron in terms of the Bohr magneton.
solution_steps: Recall the formula for the z-component of spin magnetic moment: \mu_{sz} = -g_s \mu_B m_s.
Substitute the standard values: g_s = 2 and m<sub>s</sub> = \pm 1/2.
For the maximum magnitude, take the absolute value with m_s = 1/2: |\mu_{sz, max}| = 2 \times \mu_B \times \frac{1}{2}.
Simplify the expression to find the result in terms of Bohr magneton.

solved_numericals.question: A beam of silver atoms is subjected to a magnetic field gradient \frac{\partial B_z}{\partial z} = 1.4 \times 10^2 \text{ T m}^{-1} over a pole piece length of 5.0 cm. If the velocity of atoms is 1.0 \times 10^3 \text{ m s}^{-1} and mass is 1.08 \times 10^{-25} \text{ kg}, calculate the spatial separation between the two beams on the screen placed 10 cm beyond the magnet.
solution_steps: Determine the force on the silver atom: F_z = \pm \mu_B \frac{\partial B_z}{\partial z}.
Calculate the acceleration in the magnetic field region of length L_1: a_z = \frac{F_z}{m} = \frac{\mu_B (\partial B_z / \partial z)}{m}.
Find the time spent in the magnetic field: t_1 = \frac{L_1}{v} = \frac{0.05}{10^3} = 5.0 \times 10^{-5} \text{ s}.
Calculate the transverse velocity as it exits the field: v_z = a_z t_1.
Calculate the additional deflection in the drift space of length L_2 (10 cm): y_2 = v_z \frac{L_2}{v}, and combine with deflection inside the magnet to find total separation Δz.
solved_numericals.answer: Approximately 0.2 mm (standard order of magnitude for Stern-Gerlach setups)

assumptions_and_limitations: Electron spin is a purely quantum mechanical property with no direct classical analogue; treating it as physical spinning of a charge sphere violates relativity (speed of surface would exceed c).
The Landé g-factor for spin is taken as exactly 2 in non-relativistic theory, whereas quantum electrodynamics (QED) gives a slight anomalous correction (g_s ≈ 2.00232).

common_misconceptions.wrong: An electron physically spins on its own axis just like the Earth rotates.
common_misconceptions.correct: Electron spin is an intrinsic, non-classical angular momentum.
common_misconceptions.why: Classical rotation of an electron point charge to match its spin angular momentum and magnetic moment would require surface velocities greater than the speed of light.

common_misconceptions.wrong: The spin quantum number s can take multiple integer and half-integer values like orbital quantum numbers.
common_misconceptions.correct: The spin quantum number for an electron is strictly fixed at s = 1/2.
common_misconceptions.why: Spin is an intrinsic property of the fundamental particle type, whereas orbital quantum numbers depend on the specific quantum state (n, l).

common_misconceptions.wrong: Spin-up and spin-down electrons point in completely opposite directions along all three spatial axes.
common_misconceptions.correct: Only the z-component is definite; x and y components are indeterminate.
common_misconceptions.why: Due to the commutation relations of angular momentum operators, measuring S<sub>z</sub> makes S<sub>x</sub> and S<sub>y</sub> completely uncertain.

quick_revision: Electron spin is an intrinsic angular momentum characterized by s = 1/2 and magnitude S = (√3/2)ℏ.
The z-component of spin is quantized into two states: m_s = +1/2 (spin-up) and m_s = -1/2 (spin-down).
The spin magnetic moment is proportional to the Bohr magneton with a g-factor close to 2.
The Stern-Gerlach experiment experimentally verifies the space quantization of electron spin.
Pauli's Exclusion Principle relies on half-integer spin characteristics (fermions).
